introduction: “The human world will not become a heavenly paradise through the promotion of a single matter.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá said this to people who had taken up one good cause, education or peace or the rights of women, and expected everything from it. The Bahá’í teachings, on his account and Shoghi Effendi’s, are a single body: recognition and obedience are inseparable, each principle depends on the others, and no virtue is stressed until it becomes a fault. From this the later readings draw a rule for study. Take the teachings “as a great, balanced whole”; do not set one strong statement against another, since “truth is like a jewel with many facets”; and where two passages seem to conflict, look for the link between them. The outside quotations are companions for that way of reading: Paul’s body with many members, the householder’s “things new and old,” the two proverbs about answering a fool that stand unreconciled side by side, Aristotle on wholes and on the mean, Muir’s “hitched to everything else.” Emerson, who thought consistency overrated, is the dissenting voice.
questions: Which single cause are you most tempted to think would set the world right? What does it need from the others?
“Recognition” and “observance” are called inseparable. What does each become without the other?
Find two passages in the teachings that seem to you to pull in different directions. What might be the link “somewhere in between”?
“No virtue is so over-emphasized as to become a bias or weakness.” Which virtue do you tend to over-emphasize, and what balances it?

outside.why: Other teachings are branches; these are “like the trunk of a tree which sends out all branches.” Jesus: I am the vine, ye are the branches.

“The human world will not become a heavenly paradise through the promotion of a single matter.” John Muir: when we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe.
Jesus to people who kept one part of the law with great care: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
The twin duties of recognition and obedience are “inseparable. Neither is acceptable without the other.” James: whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.

The Cause “encompasses all virtues.” Paul on reading scripture whole: all scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable; that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works.

Every prophet combines the genuine elements of the past “into a whole and adds to it new elements.” Jesus: every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old.
No one principle transforms the world. Paul: if the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing?
Believers are urged to study history, economics and sociology so as to relate the teachings to the thought of the age. Proverbs: with all thy getting get understanding.

Do not “oppose to each other two strong statements”; somewhere between are links. Proverbs sets two such statements side by side and leaves the reader to find the link: answer not a fool according to his folly. Answer a fool according to his folly.
Conceive of the teachings “as one great whole with many facets.” Aristotle: the totality is not, as it were, a mere heap, but the whole is something beside the parts.

“Truth is like a jewel with many facets. One verse may describe one facet and another, another.” The blind men at the elephant each had hold of one: each was partly in the right, and all were in the wrong.

“There is and can be no real contradiction” in the Writings; so seek the unity of meaning. Emerson took contradiction more lightly: speak what you think now in hard words and to-morrow speak what to-morrow thinks in hard words again, though it contradict every thing you said to-day. Is the reading’s rule a discipline for the reader, or a claim about the text? What would you do with a contradiction you could not resolve?
The teachings are “so perfectly balanced. No virtue is so over-emphasized as to become a bias.” Aristotle: virtue is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean.
